newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Republicans reach landmark budget deal.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Republicans reach landmark budget deal.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and the Republican leaders in Congress announced on Friday they had reached a landmark agreement on a plan to balance the U.S. federal budget by 2002.

The deal, reached after weeks of intense negotiations and years of stalemate in Washington over how to eliminate the deficit, entails cuts in a broad swathe of government programmes while offering tax cuts to benefit families and investors.

If the plan is passed by Congress, where it has opponents in both parties, and the economy grows as forecast, 2002 would mark the first time the government's accounts were in balance since 1969, when President Richard Nixon was in office.

If enacted, it would also mark a stunning breakthrough on an issue that has snarled U.S. politics for years and one that would enable both Clinton and the Republican-held Congress to claim victory over one of America's most intractable problems.

"We have reached agreement in broad but fairly specific terms ... with Republican leaders today that would balance the budget by 2002," Clinton announced during a trip to Baltimore, where he met with senators in his Democratic party.
But as both Clinton and the Republicans admitted, many details were not spelled out and those that were available will not be palatable to everyone.
The five-year budget pact requires cuts in many government programmes, including $115 billion in reductions in the popular Medicare health care programme for the elderly.
It also offers $85 billion in net tax cuts over the five years, including reductions in capital gains and estate taxes as well as a $500 per child tax credit.

News of the accord, long awaited by the financial markets, delighted Wall Street, with the Dow Jones industrial average rising 94.72 points, or 1.36 percent, to close at 7,071.20 and Treasury bonds also trading higher.
While Clinton and Republicans hailed the accord, they also quickly admitted it may be tough to sell in Congress, where hardliners in both parties object to aspects of the agreement.

"No one will look at this budget and say: 'This is perfect.' It has everything in it I want and there's nothing in it I don't like,'" Clinton said in announcing the agreement at a retreat with Senate Democrats in Baltimore, Maryland.
"But I think we've got a good shot of getting a majority of both parties in both houses, which has been my goal from day one, and if it happens, America will be much better off," he added.

"It is a compromise agreement. It had to be," said Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, who announced the agreement in the Capitol's elegant rotunda surrounded by beaming Republicans. "But it is not a compromise of our principles."
The outline agreement has already been attacked by some Democrats and Republicans and is expected to be the subject of intense negotiation in coming months.
"We have a deal, now comes the hard part -- selling it to Congress," said one senior White House official.

Although the task of cutting the government's spending is difficult at any time, Clinton and the Republican leaders of Congress have the benefit of seeking to do so at a time when the economy is growing robustly.

In one sign of the economy's health, the government said on Friday that the unemployment rate fell to 4.9 percent in April, its lowest level since 1973. Earlier in the week, the government said the economy grew by a robust 5.6 percent in the first quarter, with no sign of inflation building up.
The growth itself helps to cut the deficit, which stood at $107 billion in the last fiscal year, by raising tax revenues and limiting spending on such things as unemployment benefits.

Although the goverment's official forecast calls for the deficit to widen to $126 billion in the current fiscal year, which ends on Sept. 30, 1997, a White House official said the growth would probably lower it to the mid-$70 billion range.
White House officials told reporters that many of the pact's details had not been nailed down, including the exact terms of the planned capital gains and estate tax cuts.
